CausalChain: FGF19-driven FGFR4 overactivation -> Enhanced tumor proliferation and baseline TGF-β production -> TGF-β–mediated PD-L1 upregulation -> Partial immune restoration (with FGFR4 inhibition alone) but activation of compensatory pathways (including FGFR redundancy) -> Synergistic antitumor response upon combined FGFR4 inhibition, TGF-β blockade, and PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint inhibition, refined by digital pathology and multi-omic monitoring
Hypothesis: In FGF19-positive HCC, we hypothesize that while selective inhibition of FGFR4 diminishes tumor proliferation and modestly reduces TGF-β production (thereby lowering PD-L1 upregulation), intrinsic resistance mechanisms such as FGFR redundancy limit its therapeutic effect. Therefore, a combination treatment regimen integrating FGFR4 inhibitors with agents directly targeting TGF-β signaling and PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint blockade will synergistically enhance antitumor immune responses. This approach will leverage state-of-the-art multi-omic profiling and digital pathology to monitor treatment effectiveness in real time, ensure precise patient stratification, and enable adaptive modifications, ultimately overcoming compensatory immunosuppressive pathways for improved clinical outcomes.
Abstract: This study investigates a novel, precision-medicine based combinatorial therapeutic strategy for FGF19-positive hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Building on the established role of FGF19-driven FGFR4 overactivation in promoting tumor cell proliferation and baseline TGF-β production, which in turn facilitates PD-L1 upregulation, we hypothesize that selective FGFR4 inhibition will modestly diminish tumor proliferation and immunosuppressive signaling. However, acknowledging recent evidence of FGFR redundancy (e.g., FGFR3 and KLB interactions) that limits the efficacy of FGFR4 blockade alone, we propose that combining FGFR4 inhibitors with agents that target TGF-β signaling and PD-1/PD-L1 mediated immunosuppression will yield a synergistic antitumor response. The strategy will be optimized and continuously adapted through next-generation multi-omic profiling and digital pathology, enabling real-time monitoring of molecular changes and patient-specific adjustments.
Orignal_vs_New: The revised hypothesis retains the original causal chain steps—beginning with FGF19-driven FGFR4 overactivation leading to tumor proliferation and TGF-β production, subsequently causing PD-L1 upregulation, and acknowledging that FGFR4 inhibition alone only partially restores immune activity due to compensatory immunosuppressive mechanisms. In response to recent evidence highlighting FGFR redundancy (e.g., FGFR3, KLB interactions) as a driver of resistance, the new hypothesis expands the therapeutic scope by explicitly incorporating a stronger rationale for combination therapy. Additionally, the integration of advanced real-time multi-omic profiling and digital pathology techniques enhances the practical implementability of the approach, ensuring not only a novel combinatorial strategy but also dynamic, patient-specific treatment refinements.
